headline: Transport and hospitality sectors are struggling and reducing loan demand, while services-to-mining businesses remain healthy and continue to invest
reasoning: Callaghan notes that loan application flows at Banjo are diverging by sector. Transport and hospitality businesses are under significant stress and are not seeking loans to the same degree. In contrast, businesses providing services to the mining sector are in good shape and continuing to borrow to fund operational improvements and growth. This divergence illustrates the uneven nature of SME resilience across industries.
quote: What we're seeing is there's a lot of industries like the transport, hospitality type industries are not coming for loans as much because that they're actually in a bit of that really hurting. But then you've got businesses like services and you know services to mining and things like that, that are in a really good position. And so that's that's spending the same way as normal.
episode_title: SME resilience tested as confidence slides

headline: SMEs substituting technology and AI investment for headcount growth as wages and inflation squeeze margins
reasoning: Callaghan explains that inflation and rising wages have placed significant cost pressure on SMEs, leading them to seek efficiency through technology and AI rather than hiring more staff. He draws on Banjo Loans' own experience, noting the firm has invested heavily in technology and AI over the past 6-12 months and plans to continue doing so for the next two years, allowing them to enhance their product offering without adding headcount or cost.
quote: So, so there's there's been a lot of pressure on them with with inflation and and as we as we know that's kind of going to be their number one issue. Wages, it has been another one of those cost pressures. So, so instead of trying to throw more people at a problem, they don't, you're trying to be, see how smart they can be and how focused they can be by using technology to grow. And of course AI is coming with that.

headline: Rise in SMEs carrying ATO debt from 19% to 23% reflects deliberate cash flow management rather than systemic stress, with most on formal repayment plans
reasoning: Callaghan characterises the increase in ATO debt among SMEs as a long-standing cash-flow management technique used since accountants have been around, treating the ATO as a de facto short-term lender. He notes that most SMEs recognise when they have accumulated ATO debt and proactively put themselves on payment plans to reduce it. He views this as an ebb and flow of business rather than a sign of systemic cracks, consistent with his observation that SME borrowers are diligent about meeting repayment obligations.
quote: Look, I think that has been a form of cash flow management since as long as accountants have been around, to be honest, they've used sort of Ato as a slight, slight bank, let's say. But but what, what they're doing is they're being really smarter about it. Now when they realise that they have gone into Ato debt, the majority of SMEs are putting themselves on a plan to actually take that dip down and get themselves back into a comfortable position.

headline: SME long-term confidence has softened but 68% hit revenue targets and 72% expect to do so in the year ahead; revenue targets may have been quietly adjusted downward
reasoning: Guy Callaghan notes that SME business owners are inherently optimistic and typically glass three-quarters full. While long-term confidence has fallen, a high proportion of SMEs are still meeting revenue targets, though he suspects those targets may have been modestly revised down in line with the economic downturn. Banjo Loans is seeing a high volume of working capital loan applications, suggesting businesses still want to grow, but loan quality is not as strong as previously.
quote: Yeah, really good question. All right, look, I've always said this, that it's me. Business owners are glass 3/4 full. They always look for the positives. They always see how they can improve themselves and see ways they can grow. Probably the one thing we haven't seen here and there's one thing that's not in the data is have they changed their revenue targets to be hit or you know, have they adjusted that slightly with the downturn? Because what we're seeing is we're getting a lot of applications through the door. So a lot of businesses are coming to us applying for working capital loans, which means they're wanting to grow, they're wanting to take that next step and how they can improve, but the qualities not as high as what it used to be previously.

headline: Almost half of SMEs plan to lift prices over the next 12 months as pricing becomes the last lever available after years of cost-cutting
reasoning: Callaghan argues that after roughly five years of difficult conditions, SMEs have already exhausted most levers — cutting product ranges, sharpening operations, reducing costs — and pricing is now the primary remaining tool. Rising wages, supply chain costs, and fuel have compounded the pressure, making price increases both a survival mechanism and a margin protection strategy. This is consistent with a survey Banjo conducted six months ago.
quote: I think after a number of years, I've sort of five years of, of really tough conditions for, for SM ES without tried everything. They've pulled a lot of levers like cutting down the products they offer, sharpening their operation, cutting on costs of operation, all that type of stuff. Now they're getting to the point where the one of the only levers I've got to pull to really survive, you know, because I've got things like increased increased wages, increased costs on supply chain fuel, all that type of thing. Probably the final leader that I've got to pull is pricing.

headline: Banjo Loans sees stable SME arrears despite tough economic conditions, flagging 'alert but not alarmed' posture
reasoning: Guy Callaghan notes that arrears across Banjo Loans' SME borrower base have remained consistent over the past three years despite a difficult economic environment post-COVID. He attributes this stability to business owners being highly attuned to their cash flows and meeting their financial commitments diligently. The major banks have been monitoring SME stress closely and have been in dialogue with Banjo, but Callaghan says the outcome has been pleasing. Post-budget, he characterises activity as 'business as usual,' noting the CGT changes don't materially affect Banjo's lending focus (cash flow lending rather than business sale finance), and that the instant asset write-off extension was largely already expected by the market.
quote: Look. And that's something we've been really, um, we've been really monitoring quite, um, diligently. I mean, we always do. But, you know, as I said, some of the majors are concerned, so, so that that sort of chatting to us, but we're, we're monitoring it really diligently and probably our, our saying at the moment is we're, we're alert, but we're not alarmed. And pleasingly, we are just seeing business as usual with arrears. And I think what that means is, you know, we had Covid a while back and then we have had a really tough economy and business owners are really attuned to it, and they actually know their cash flow really well. And as a consequence, they're really attuned to the cash commitments that they've got and being really diligent about keeping them up there.
episode_title: A new era for SME finance
